text: A black hole is an astronomical object so dense that its gravity prevents anything, including light, from escaping. Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity predicts that a sufficiently compact mass will form a black hole. The boundary beyond which nothing can escape is called the event horizon; in general relativity, crossing it causes no locally detectable change but seals an object's fate. The theory also predicts that every black hole has a central singularity where spacetime curvature becomes infinite. Black holes behave like ideal black bodies, reflecting no light. Quantum field theory in curved spacetime predicts that event horizons emit Hawking radiation with a black-body spectrum, where temperature is inversely proportional to mass—about billionths of a kelvin for stellar black holes, making direct observation essentially impossible. The concept of a body with such strong gravity that light cannot escape was first proposed in the 18th century by John Michell and independently by Pierre-Simon Laplace, who considered very large stars rather than extremely dense objects. Michell calculated that a star with 500 times the Sun’s radius and the same density would have an escape velocity exceeding the speed of light and could be detected through gravitational effects on nearby bodies. Laplace similarly suggested invisible stars in 1796, though he omitted this in later editions due to doubts about the corpuscular theory of light. In 1905, Einstein established the principle of special relativity, showing that electromagnetism is invariant under Lorentz transformations, while in 1911 he predicted light deflection by massive bodies, though his calculation was off by a factor of two. By 1917, Einstein developed general relativity, which describes how matter affects spacetime and how spacetime influences matter, forming the foundation for black hole physics. Karl Schwarzschild, shortly after Einstein published his field equations, found the first solution describing a black hole under spherical symmetry and no spin; this solution, known as the Schwarzschild metric, was later independently derived by Johannes Droste. At a certain radius—the Schwarzschild radius—the solution becomes singular, a feature not fully understood at the time. Many physicists in the early 20th century were skeptical of black holes; Arthur Eddington discussed the idea in 1926 but dismissed it as a theoretical issue, and Einstein himself attempted in 1939 to prove black holes were impossible by relying on pressure or centrifugal forces to counter gravity, missing the possibility of collapse below the Schwarzschild radius. In the 1920s, astronomers found white dwarf stars too cool and dense for standard stellar cooling models; Ralph Fowler showed that quantum degeneracy pressure exceeds thermal pressure at such densities. Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar calculated in 1931 that a non-rotating electron-degenerate star below a certain mass—now called the Chandrasekhar limit (1.4 M☉)—is stable, and by 1934 this explained white dwarf observations. At a meeting where he presented this, Eddington claimed stars above this limit would collapse into non-radiating bodies, a conclusion he considered absurd, and later, with Lev Landau, argued that an unknown force would halt collapse—partially correct, as stars slightly above the limit collapse into neutron stars. In the 1930s, Fritz Zwicky and Walter Baade studied supernovae, proposing that they produce neutron stars, an idea largely ignored. In 1937, Lev Landau developed a nuclear core model that attracted Robert Oppenheimer, who, in 1939, with George Volkoff, predicted that neutron stars below a certain mass—now the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit—would be stable due to neutron degeneracy pressure, while above that limit gravitational collapse would continue. John Archibald Wheeler and his students, including Harrison and Wakano, studied the TOV limit and found no features invalidating it, concluding that the only way to prevent black hole formation would be a dynamic process ejecting mass. Wheeler believed neutrons in an imploding star would convert to radiation quickly, preventing black hole formation. In 1939, Oppenheimer and Hartland Snyder published a paper solving Einstein’s equations for an imploding star, now known as the Oppenheimer–Snyder model; they showed that as the star collapses, gravitational time dilation causes the implosion to appear to slow down and freeze at the Schwarzschild radius from a distant observer’s view. In 1958, David Finkelstein identified the Schwarzschild surface as an event horizon, describing it as a "perfect unidirectional membrane" where causal influences can only pass in one direction, and he introduced a new reference frame for infalling observers. This concept, later expanded by Martin Kruskal, was fully reconciled by 1962, convincing many skeptics that black hole formation was physically valid. From the mid-1960s to mid-1970s, black hole research experienced a "golden age," during which more general solutions were found: in 1963, Roy Kerr discovered the rotating black hole solution, and in 1965, Ezra Newman found a solution for a rotating, charged black hole. In 1967, Werner Israel proved that the Schwarzschild solution is the only possible one for a nonspinning, uncharged black hole, defined solely by mass; later, it was shown that Reissner-Nordstrom black holes are defined by mass and charge, and Kerr black holes by mass and spin. Together, these findings form the no-hair theorem, stating that a stationary black hole is completely described by mass, angular momentum, and electric charge. Initially, some physicists like Vladimir Belinski, Isaak Khalatnikov, and Evgeny Lifshitz believed singularities were artifacts of spherical symmetry and would not appear in generic cases, but in 1965 Roger Penrose proved that general relativity requires singularities in all black holes, and Hawking later generalized this to show that a cosmological Big Bang singularity is inevitable unless quantum gravity intervenes. In 1967, Antony Hewish and Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered pulsars, which were later shown to be rapidly rotating neutron stars, proving the physical reality of neutron stars and sparking interest in compact objects. Based on observations in the early 1970s, Cygnus X-1, a galactic X-ray source discovered in 1964, became the first widely accepted black hole. In 1972, Louise Webster, Paul Murdin, and Charles Thomas Bolton found that Cygnus X-1 was in a binary system with the supergiant star HDE 226868, and that its mass was too large to be a white dwarf or neutron star, indicating it was likely a black hole. By the end of 1973, Cygnus X-1 was generally accepted as a black hole. While supermassive black holes were theorized as early as the 1960s by Donald Lynden-Bell and Martin Rees to power quasars, observational proof was lacking until the Hubble Space Telescope revealed that nearly every galaxy has a supermassive black hole at its center, many of which are quiescent. In 1999, David Merritt proposed the M–sigma relation, linking the velocity dispersion in a galaxy’s central bulge to the mass of its supermassive black hole, a correlation later confirmed. Around the same time, independent teams led by Andrea Ghez and Reinhard Genzel used observations of stars near the Milky Way’s center to conclude that the compact radio source Sagittarius A* contained a supermassive black hole of about 4.3 million solar masses. On 11 February 2016, the LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration announced the first direct detection of gravitational waves, named GW150914, marking the first observation of a black hole merger. At the time of the merger, the black holes were about 1.4 billion light-years away and had masses of 30 and 35 solar masses.

The term appeared in print in Life and Science News magazines in 1963 and in Ann Ewing’s article "'Black Holes' in Space," published on 18 January 1964.[29] A black hole is generally defined as a region of spacetime from which no information-carrying signals or objects can escape,[99] but verifying this would require infinite time and distance, making it impractical for identification.[100] There is no universally agreed-upon definition; among astrophysicists, a black hole is a compact object with a mass greater than four solar masses.[101] It may also be defined as a reservoir of information[102]: 142  or a region where space falls inward faster than light.[103][104] The no-hair theorem states that a stable black hole has only three properties: mass, electric charge, and angular momentum; any two black holes with identical values for these are indistinguishable, though the validity of this conjecture for real black holes remains unresolved.[41] The simplest static black holes have mass but no charge or angular momentum and are known as Schwarzschild black holes, discovered by Karl Schwarzschild in 1916; according to Birkhoff's theorem, it is the only spherically symmetric vacuum solution.[105] More general solutions include the Reissner–Nordström metric for non-rotating charged black holes, the Kerr metric for non-charged rotating black holes, and the Kerr–Newman metric for black holes with both charge and angular momentum.[106] From a distant perspective, a black hole's external gravitational field is identical to that of any other object of the same mass, contrary to the popular idea that it "sucks in everything."[107] While a black hole can theoretically have any positive mass, its charge and angular momentum are constrained by mass. The total electric charge Q and angular momentum J must satisfy the inequality Q²/(4πϵ₀) + c²J²/(GM²) ≤ GM² for a black hole of mass M. Black holes with maximum charge or spin satisfying this are called extremal black holes. Solutions violating the inequality exist but lack an event horizon and are termed naked singularities, which could make the universe unpredictable; many physicists believe they cannot exist.[108][109] The weak cosmic censorship hypothesis, proposed by Sir Roger Penrose, suggests that such singularities are ruled out during the gravitational collapse of realistic matter, though this has not been proven and some physicists believe naked singularities could exist.[110] It is also unknown whether black holes could become extremal, as natural processes counteract increasing spin and charge when near-extremal.[110][111][112] The total mass of a black hole can be estimated from the motion of nearby objects such as stars or gas.[66] All black holes spin, often rapidly—GRS 1915+105 spins over 1,000 times per second,[113][114] and Sagittarius A* rotates at about 90% of its maximum rate.[115][116] Spin can be inferred from X-ray spectral lines as gas plunges inward, producing redshifted emission due to relativistic effects; the radius of the plunge varies with spin, allowing astronomers to determine the spin from the gap between outer disk emission and redshifted plunging material.[117] A newer method estimates spin from the temperature of accreting gas, requiring independent measurements of mass and disk inclination, followed by computer modeling. Gravitational waves from merging black holes can also provide spin information, though such events are rare.[117] A spinning black hole has angular momentum; the supermassive black hole in M87 appears to have angular momentum very close to the theoretical maximum.[115][118][119] The uncharged limit is J ≤ GM²/c, allowing a dimensionless spin parameter such that 0 ≤ cJ/(GM²) ≤ 1.[120][121] Most black holes are believed to be approximately neutral; Michal Zajaček et al. found the charge of Sagittarius A* to be at least ten orders of magnitude below its theoretical maximum.[122] A charged black hole repels like charges, similar to any charged object; if charged, opposite charges are pulled in and like charges are repelled, leading to neutralization, which may be less effective if the black hole is also spinning.[123][124] Charge in a nonspinning black hole is bounded by Q ≤ √(G)M.[126] Black holes vary widely in mass. Black holes are rapidly gaining mass, and all black holes with jets possess an accretion disk, though jets are typically brighter than the disk. Supermassive black holes with jets are known as quasars or "macroquasars" and are observed in other galaxies, while stellar-mass black holes with jets, commonly seen in the Milky Way, are called microquasars. The exact mechanism of jet formation remains unknown, but the Blandford-Znajek process proposes that the rotation of a black hole drags magnetic field lines, launching matter into space, and the Penrose process suggests that rotational energy can be extracted to power jets. Due to conservation of angular momentum, gas falling into a massive object forms a disk-like structure; as angular momentum is transferred outward, matter spirals inward, converting gravitational energy into heat and emitting intense x-rays. Accretion disk temperatures range from thousands to millions of Kelvin and vary across the disk, with emissions extending into other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum depending on turbulence, magnetization, and black hole properties. Disks are classified as geometrically thin (confined to the equatorial plane with a defined edge at the innermost stable circular orbit, or ISCO) or geometrically thick (supported by internal pressure and extending inside the ISCO). Optically thick disks are bright and opaque, while optically thin disks are translucent and faint. Accretion disks exceeding the Eddington limit are called "polish donuts" due to their thick, toroidal shape. Quasar accretion disks are generally blue, while stellar black hole disks appear orange, yellow, or red, with inner regions being brightest; theoretical expectations of hotter disks being bluer are not always confirmed by observations. Doppler effects alter disk colors, with approaching parts appearing bluer and brighter and receding parts redder and dimmer. In Newtonian gravity, stable orbits exist at any distance, but general relativity introduces a minimum stable orbit—the ISCO—where any small inward or outward perturbation leads to inward spiral. For a Schwarzschild black hole (zero spin), the ISCO is at 3 times the Schwarzschild radius (6GM/c²), and this radius shifts based on particle spin: for retrograde orbits, it can extend to about 9rs, while prograde orbits can reach the event horizon. For charged black holes, the ISCO moves inward. The photon sphere, where photons orbit tangentially, has a radius of 1.5 times the Schwarzschild radius for Schwarzschild black holes and at least that for non-Schwarzschild black holes; light rays with impact parameters below this radius fall into the black hole. From afar, the photon sphere creates an observable black hole shadow, the limit of detectable light, and colliding black holes may have identifiable shadow shapes. Light emitted from within the photon sphere must originate between it and the event horizon, and light directed toward it can curve back to the observer. For rotating black holes, the photon sphere radius varies with spin and orbit direction: prograde orbits occur at 1–3rs, retrograde at 3–5rs. Charged, nonrotating black holes have one photon sphere whose radius decreases with increasing charge, while non-extremal, charged, rotating black holes have two photon spheres. Near rotating black holes, spacetime drags matter and light into rotation—a phenomenon called frame dragging—creating an ergosphere where space moves faster than light. The ergosphere, bounded by the event horizon and ergosurface, allows matter and radiation to escape, and the Penrose process enables objects to emerge with more energy than they entered, extracting rotational energy from the black hole. The Blandford–Znajek process, involving strong magnetic fields, is considered a likely explanation for the luminosity and relativistic jets of quasars and active galactic nuclei. The plunging region, closest to the event horizon, is where free-falling matter cannot maintain circular orbits and rapidly descends at near-light speed, heating up and emitting detectable thermal radiation. Light from this region can still escape. The defining feature of a black hole is the event horizon, a boundary beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape; events within it cannot affect outside observers. General relativity predicts that mass deforms spacetime, bending particle paths, and at the event horizon, this deformation becomes so extreme that no paths lead away. To a distant observer, a clock near a black hole appears to tick more slowly, and an object falling in appears to slow, fade, and redshift, disappearing within one hundredth of a second from a distance of half a Schwarzschild radius above the horizon, flattening onto the black hole. An observer falling in does not notice these effects at the event horizon, as their own clocks tick normally and they cross it in finite time, with no local detection of the horizon due to the equivalence principle. For non-rotating black holes, the event horizon is spherical, while rotating ones are oblate. Rotating or charged black holes have an inner horizon, or Cauchy horizon, divided into ingoing and outgoing sections. At the ingoing section, radiation and matter build up, causing infinite spacetime curvature and tidal forces—known as mass inflation or mass-inflation singularity—while at the outgoing section, infalling radiation backscatters, building up and causing a gravitational shock wave and tidal forces—called the shock singularity. Both singularities are weak, meaning finite tidal deformation occurs despite infinite curvature, and are null singularities, allowing photons to pass parallel without interception. General relativity predicts singularities at black hole centers—points of infinite curvature and zero volume where geodesics end—though it is uncertain if they exist in real black holes. Some physicists argue singularities signal a breakdown of general relativity and the need for quantum gravity, while others believe they can be resolved within current physics or that they do not exist due to quantum effects. Kip Thorne and Charles Misner believe some singularities may still exist. For non-rotating black holes, the singularity is a point; for rotating ones, it is a ring in the plane of rotation. All mass ends in the singularity, giving it infinite density. Observers falling into a Schwarzschild black hole cannot avoid the singularity and are torn apart by tidal forces—a process known as spaghettification—eventually being crushed to a point. Before the 1970s, it was thought the interior curved inward to a sharp point, but Belinskii, Khalatnikov, and Lifshitz found that perturbations cause chaotic oscillations near the singularity, termed "Mixmaster dynamics," resembling an electric mixer's effect on dough. For charged or rotating black holes, it may be possible to avoid the singularity, with theoretical models suggesting exit into another spacetime via a wormhole, though perturbations destroy this possibility. Closed timelike curves around the Kerr singularity could allow time travel, leading to causality issues like the grandfather paradox, though quantum gravity effects or mass inflation may prevent them. Some gravity models eliminate singularities, resulting in regular or nonsingular black holes; for example, the fuzzball model in string theory suggests black holes consist of quantum microstates without singularities or event horizons, and loop quantum gravity proposes finite curvature and density at the center. Black holes form through gravitational collapse of massive stars via direct collapse or supernova "fallback," or through mergers of two neutron stars or a neutron star and a black hole.

Returning to one's own past around the Kerr singularity can lead to causality problems such as the grandfather paradox. However, processes inside black holes, like quantum gravity effects or mass inflation, might prevent closed timelike curves from forming. Some models of gravity avoid black hole singularities altogether, resulting in theoretical black holes known as regular or nonsingular black holes. For instance, the fuzzball model, based on string theory, suggests black holes consist of quantum microstates and do not require a singularity or an event horizon. Loop quantum gravity proposes that the curvature and density at the center of a black hole are large but finite. Black holes form through the gravitational collapse of massive stars, either via direct collapse or during a supernova explosion known as "fallback," or through the merger of two neutron stars or a neutron star and a black hole. Other speculative mechanisms include primordial black holes formed from density fluctuations in the early universe, the collapse of dark stars, or from hypothetical self-interacting dark matter. Gravitational collapse occurs when an object's internal pressure fails to counteract its own gravity; at the end of a star's life, it fuses elements up to iron, and fusion stops because fusing heavier elements consumes more energy than it releases. If the iron core is too massive, the star collapses under gravity. While most energy from collapse is released quickly, a distant observer never sees the collapse complete—infalling matter appears to slow and freeze just above the event horizon due to gravitational time dilation, with light from the material becoming infinitely delayed and redshifted, causing the object to fade. Observations of quasars at redshift z ∼ 7, less than a billion years after the Big Bang, have prompted investigations into alternative black hole formation pathways. The accretion process to build supermassive black holes has a mass accumulation limit, and a billion years is insufficient to reach quasar status. One suggestion is the direct collapse of nearly pure hydrogen gas clouds with low metallicity, forming a supermassive star that collapses into a black hole, potentially producing seed black holes of ~10⁵ M☉ that grow to ~10⁹ M☉. However, such gas is not typically stable against fragmentation into multiple stars. An alternative involves massive star formation followed by collisions that seed massive black holes, which then merge to form a quasar. A neutron star in a common envelope with a regular star or two neutron stars merging can also form a black hole, though these processes are considered relatively rare. In the current universe, black hole formation is rare and mostly occurs in stars, but in the early universe, conditions may have allowed formation through other means. Fluctuations in spacetime shortly after the Big Bang could have created denser regions that eventually collapsed into black holes. Models vary in predicting the scale of these fluctuations, with primordial black holes ranging from a Planck mass (~2.2×10⁻⁸ kg) to hundreds of thousands of solar masses. Primordial black holes with masses below 10¹⁵ g would have evaporated by now due to Hawking radiation. Despite the early universe's high density, it did not re-collapse into a black hole because it expanded rapidly and lacked the necessary gravitational differential. Models for constant-sized objects like stars do not apply directly to rapidly expanding space such as the Big Bang. In principle, black holes could form in high-energy particle collisions achieving sufficient density, though no such events have been detected. Hypothetical micro black holes from cosmic ray collisions or particle accelerators like the Large Hadron Collider would not accumulate mass and would evaporate in about 10⁻²⁵ seconds, posing no threat to Earth. Once formed, black holes grow by absorbing surrounding matter, a process thought to contribute to the formation of supermassive black holes, though this remains an open research area. A similar mechanism may explain intermediate-mass black holes in globular clusters. Black holes can also merge with stars or other black holes, a process believed to have been important in the early growth of supermassive black holes and possibly in forming some intermediate-mass black holes. Growth is limited by the Eddington limit, where radiation pressure balances gravity, preventing further accretion; however, many black holes accrete beyond this rate due to non-spherical geometry or disk instabilities, a phenomenon called super-Eddington accretion, which may have been common in the early universe. Mergers of supermassive black holes face the "final parsec problem," where binary systems take a long time to merge because nearby stars are ejected, leaving little material for gravitational interaction, with the final separation typically around one parsec. When matter accretes, the inner accretion disk orbits at high speeds, generating significant friction that heats it to emit vast electromagnetic radiation, primarily X-rays. Between 5.7% and 42% of the matter's mass is converted to energy, depending on the black hole's spin, with about 90% released within 20 black hole radii. In many cases, relativistic jets are emitted along the poles, though their origin is not well understood. Many of the universe's most energetic events are attributed to black hole accretion, including active galactic nuclei and quasars, which are believed to be accretion disks of supermassive black holes. X-ray binaries are generally binary systems where one star is a compact object accreting matter from its companion, and some ultraluminous X-ray sources may be accretion disks of intermediate-mass black holes. Tidal disruption events occur when stars are torn apart by tidal forces near supermassive black holes, with some material forming an accretion disk that emits detectable radiation. The correlation between supermassive black hole masses and the velocity dispersion and mass of stars in galactic bulges suggests a link between galaxy and black hole formation. Black hole winds from rapid accretion can compress nearby gas, stimulating star formation, but if too strong, they can expel gas and halt star formation. Jets may also energize plasma cavities and eject low-entropy gas, heating the galactic center. In 1974, Stephen Hawking predicted black holes emit thermal radiation at a temperature of ℏc³/(8πGMkB), where ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, c is the speed of light, G is the gravitational constant, M is the black hole's mass, and kB is the Boltzmann constant. This effect, known as Hawking radiation, arises from applying quantum field theory to black holes and was supported by Jacob Bekenstein's theory that black holes have entropy proportional to their surface area and thus a temperature. This is analogous to the Unruh effect, where an accelerating observer detects a higher temperature than a non-accelerating one, with the temperature matching that of an observer near a black hole's horizon. Many physicists have verified this result through various methods. If correct, black holes shrink and evaporate over time as they emit photons and particles. The Hawking temperature is inversely proportional to mass, so larger black holes emit less radiation. A 1 M☉ stellar black hole has a Hawking temperature of 62 nanokelvins, far below the 2.7 K cosmic microwave background temperature. Larger black holes gain more mass from the background radiation than they lose, so they grow. A black hole must have a mass less than that of the Moon to have a Hawking temperature above 2.7 K and thus evaporate, with such a black hole having a diameter less than a tenth of a millimeter. Very small black holes emit strongly; a car-mass black hole has a diameter of about 10⁻²⁴ m and evaporates in a nanosecond, briefly shining brighter than the Sun. For even smaller black holes, quantum gravity effects may stabilize them, though current quantum gravity theories do not support this. Hawking radiation from astrophysical black holes is extremely weak and difficult to detect from Earth. A possible exception is gamma-ray bursts from the final evaporation of primordial black holes. Searches have found no such bursts, placing strict limits on the existence of low-mass primordial black holes, with modern estimates suggesting they make up less than 10⁻⁷ of the universe's total mass. NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope has searched for these flashes without success. A non-accreting solar mass black hole would evaporate over 10⁶⁴ years, while a supermassive black hole of 10¹¹ M☉ would take around 2×10¹⁰⁰ years. During a supercluster collapse, supermassive black holes may grow to 10¹⁴ M☉, still evaporating over up to 10¹⁰⁶ years. The end of evaporation is unknown; some physicists suggest a remnant like a naked singularity. Millions of black holes with about 30 solar masses from stellar collapse are expected in the Milky Way, with dwarf galaxies like Draco containing hundreds. Only a few have been detected. Black holes do not emit electromagnetic radiation except for hypothetical Hawking radiation, so their detection relies on indirect observations. The defining feature is the event horizon, which cannot be imaged directly; all alternative explanations must be ruled out before concluding a black hole is present. The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) is a global network of radio telescopes capable of imaging a black hole's shadow. In April 2017, EHT began observing the black hole at the center of Messier 87. Using petabytes of data from eight radio observatories over ten days, the team created a composite image released in April 2019. The image shows a dark circle—the black hole's shadow—surrounded by an orange-red ring of its accretion disk. The bottom half of the disk is brighter than the top due to Doppler beaming: material at the bottom moves toward the observer at relativistic speeds, appearing brighter. In April 2023, the EHT presented the first image of the Messier 87 black hole's shadow and its high-energy jet together. On 12 May 2022, the EHT released the first image of Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way. The team had previously detected magnetic field lines around it, confirming theoretical predictions. The imaging was done simultaneously with M87*. Like M87*, Sagittarius A*'s shadow and accretion disk are visible, with the shadow size matching theoretical models. Imaging Sagittarius A* was more complex due to its instability—being one thousand times less massive than M87*, its accretion disk has a much shorter orbital period, causing rapid environmental changes during observation. Turbulent plasma between Sagittarius A* and Earth also hinders resolution at longer wavelengths. On 14 September 2015, LIGO made the first direct detection of gravitational waves, consistent with signals from the merger of two black holes: one with about 36 solar masses and the other around 29 solar masses. Because the objects were only 350 km apart just before merging and were more massive than possible for neutron stars, the signal must have originated from a black hole merger. The signal also included the start of the post-merger phase.

In 2015, the LIGO gravitational wave observatory made the first direct observation of gravitational waves, consistent with the merger of two black holes—one with about 36 solar masses and the other around 29 solar masses—detecting a signal that included the post-merger ringdown, which revealed the resulting black hole had a mass of 62 solar masses, was spinning at 67% of the maximum rate, and lost three solar masses as gravitational waves during the merger. This observation provided the first observational evidence for stellar-mass black hole binaries and confirmed the existence of stellar-mass black holes weighing 25 solar masses or more. Since then, many more gravitational wave events have been detected. Observations of stars near the Milky Way’s center show they orbit an invisible object coincident with Sagittarius A*, with 90 stars tracked since 1995; by fitting their motions to Keplerian orbits, astronomers inferred that Sagittarius A* must be a 2.6×10⁶ M☉ object within a radius of 0.02 light-years. After one full orbit of the star S2, the mass of Sagittarius A* was refined to 4.3×10⁶ M☉ with a radius less than 0.002 light-years, an upper limit larger than the Schwarzschild radius, which does not prove it is a black hole but strongly suggests one, with some evidence for an event horizon. The 2022 Event Horizon Telescope image of Sagittarius A* further confirmed it is a black hole. X-ray binaries emit X-rays when a compact object accretes matter from a normal star, and by measuring orbital period, distance, and companion star mass, scientists can estimate the compact object’s mass; the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit sets a maximum mass of about two solar masses for a nonrotating neutron star, and masses exceeding this are generally considered black holes. Cygnus X-1, discovered in 1972 by Charles Thomas Bolton, Louise Webster, and Paul Murdin, was the first strong black hole candidate, with a mass estimate of 16 solar masses in 1986 and later updated to 14.1±1.0 M☉ for the black hole and 19.2±1.9 M☉ for the companion. X-ray binaries are classified as low-mass or high-mass based on the companion star’s mass, with soft X-ray transients allowing accurate black hole mass estimates during quiescence. Black holes are also found in binaries with white dwarfs, neutron stars, or other black holes. Nearly every galaxy contains a supermassive black hole, and the M–sigma relation links the black hole’s mass to the velocity dispersion of the galaxy’s bulge, suggesting a connection between black hole and galaxy formation. Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are powered by accretion onto supermassive black holes and include a central black hole, an accretion disk, and two perpendicular jets. Notable galaxies with supermassive black hole candidates include Andromeda, Messier 32, Messier 87, the Sombrero Galaxy, and the Milky Way. Quasi-periodic oscillations in X-ray emissions from accretion disks are thought to arise from material near the innermost stable circular orbit or from misalignment between the black hole’s rotation and the binary’s axis, and their frequency correlates with the black hole’s mass and spin, allowing estimation of these properties. Black holes can also be detected via gravitational lensing, where their strong gravity bends light, creating distorted images or multiple images of background sources; microlensing occurs when the lensing object is a black hole, causing a temporary brightening of a star as the black hole moves between the star and Earth, with the first confirmed detection of such an event occurring in January 2022, yielding a mass of 7.1±1.3 M☉ for an isolated black hole. While stellar-mass black holes are assumed to form when objects exceed the neutron star mass limit, exotic matter phases like quark stars or electroweak stars could support massive objects via degeneracy pressure, with quark stars being the only viable alternative that could exceed neutron star limits. Theoretical objects such as dark energy stars, black stars, and gravastars have been proposed as alternatives to black holes, functioning through different mechanisms. Supermassive black holes are less dense than stellar black holes, with a 10⁸ M☉ black hole having a density comparable to water, and alternative models like large clusters of dark objects are generally unstable and not viable. According to the no-hair theorem, black holes are defined by only mass, charge, and angular momentum, implying all other information about the matter that formed them is lost, leading to the black hole information paradox: Hawking radiation appears to convert a pure quantum state into a mixed state, violating unitarity in quantum mechanics, while general relativity’s equivalence principle suggests such destruction cannot occur at the event horizon. This paradox remains unresolved and is central to developing a theory of quantum gravity. Observations of distant galaxies have found ultraluminous quasars at redshifts z ≥ 7, powered by supermassive black holes, which are thought to originate from the gravitational collapse of large population III stars, though these stars were not massive enough to produce such quasars without accreting beyond the Eddington limit. Proposed formation mechanisms include mergers of smaller black holes, direct-collapse black holes from large, low-angular-momentum gas clouds forming a single supermassive star, or primordial black holes that accreted matter. Some mechanisms allow black holes to grow faster than the Eddington limit, such as dense gas in the accretion disk reducing radiation pressure, though bipolar jets prevent super-Eddington accretion. Black holes have been featured in science fiction since the 1920s, including in The Skylark of Space and Starship Invincible, and have since appeared in films and novels like Disney’s The Black Hole (1979) and Christopher Nolan’s Interstellar (2014), where relativistic effects such as gravitational time dilation are used, with Interstellar featuring a time dilation factor of over 60,000:1 and other works depicting black holes as wormholes or hazards to space travel.
